title: Drug-fuelled seizure killed crazed intruder: Playwright admits folly of tackling man
article: Playwright Marty Chan called himself "the dumbest man in the world" Tuesday for tackling a crazed intruder who smashed up his house in a cocaine-fuelled rampage.

It took four police officers to subdue Richard Bellerose on the front yard of Chan's Forest Heights home before Bellerose suddenly stopped breathing, killed in a massive, drug-induced adrenaline rush.
Chan testified at a fatality inquiry that he and his wife, Michelle, awoke about 2:45 a.m. July 27, 2002, to the sound of their back door being kicked in.

Once inside, Bellerose smashed an end table against the wall, threw another table through the kitchen window and ruined curtains with bloody hand prints before crashing out the front screen door, Chan said.

Chan, author of several hit Fringe Festival plays, jumped the six- foot-tall, 203-pound stranger as he stumbled outside. But he discovered stopping Bellerose was going to be difficult when punches to his head and groin had no effect.
"I realized he was going to be too strong for me. I tried grabbing his wrists and pinning him down as best I could. All the time, he was yelling obscenities."
Chan held on for several minutes until police arrived. He went inside to help his wife tend to a cut on her wrist caused by broken glass.
With no training in hand-to-hand fighting, he couldn't say exactly what led him to take on the trespasser.

"I was the dumbest man in the world. I was thinking this man had entered my home ... heard my wife scream, didn't know what had happened, thought this man was responsible and I thought I should do something."

The first two police officers on the scene testified Bellerose, 30, was unusually aggressive as they wrestled to put him in handcuffs. Two more officers soon arrived. As Bellerose continued to struggle, they bound his legs together.

When it became obvious he wasn't breathing a short time later, they removed the handcuffs and freed his legs so he could be treated by ambulance staff. He was declared dead in hospital from what Alberta's chief medical examiner Dr. Graeme Dowling described as cocaine toxicity.

Dowling listed the use of the restraint used on Bellrose's legs as an associated factor in the death, but said it's "virtually impossible" to tell what role it might have played. A person with excited delirium "will exhibit superhuman strength such that quite often it will take six or seven strong adults to hold the person down," he said.
